content: Zedoary, scientifically known as Curcuma zedoaria and referred to as kacōramu in Telugu, is a perennial herb belonging to the genus Curcuma Linn and the family Zingiberaceae. This plant is indigenous to India and Indonesia. It was introduced to Europe by Arab traders around the sixth century. However, its use as a spice in Western cuisine has become exceedingly rare, as it has largely been replaced by ginger. Zedoary is a rhizomatous plant that thrives in tropical and subtropical wet forest regions. The plant produces fragrant yellow flowers accompanied by red and green bracts. Its underground stem, or rhizome, is large, tuberous, and extensively branched. The leaf shoots of the plant are elongated and can grow up to 1 meter (approximately 3 feet) in height. The edible root of zedoary has a white interior and emits a fragrance reminiscent of mango. However, its taste is more akin to ginger, with the notable distinction of a pronounced bitter aftertaste. In Indonesia, the root is typically dried, ground into a powder, and incorporated into curry pastes. In contrast, in India, it is more commonly used in its fresh form or pickled. Zedoary also holds a place in traditional Eastern medicine, where it is believed to aid digestion, alleviate colic, and act as a blood purifier. Additionally, the essential oil extracted from the dried roots of Curcuma zedoaria is utilized in the production of perfumes and soaps. It is also an ingredient in the formulation of bitter tonics.
